text: One of the biggest mistakes I see founders make is relying on aggregate user metrics instead of understanding how any individual users use their product.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: In my last video, I talked about cohort retention curves and how you can use those to separate groups of users and track what they do over time throughout using your product.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And I think that's the best tool that you've got to figure out if people keep using your product.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: But what you don't know is how are they using your product?
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: How are they interacting?
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: What features are they using?
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: What's the frequency of use?
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: What's the pacing of how they use the product?
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And most founders just ignore this, but I think it's the most important signal to figure out if you've built something that people want.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So you want to be able to look at what individual users are doing, but that's a lot.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Right?
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: If you even have like 10 or 20 users, it's pretty challenging to just tail the logs and watch every event that every user is doing.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So with aggregate data, the graphs that we're all used to talking about, things like DAUs or MAUs, these lump all of your users together and you can't really get a sense of what any individual user is doing.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And if you have any amount of growth, those graphs tend to be going up and to the right, even if users aren't actually enjoying using your product.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So today I want to tell you about a tool that we came to in my startup that allows you to understand what's going on with individual users while also giving you a big picture view of how your entire product is performing.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And we call it the dot plot.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So let me show you what a dot plot looks like.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Based on the name, you can figure out it probably involves dots.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: What you basically do is just make a two-dimensional grid, like a spreadsheet, where there are a bunch of columns and a bunch of rows.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Each row represents one individual user.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: If I'm one of the users, I'll write my name here.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Dave, I'm one of the users.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And every other user of your product gets their own row.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And then every column represents a time period.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: I think days are usually the right thing to use for your product, but it probably depends a bit on the nature of your product.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So let's just draw in the days.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: I'll just do Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And you can make this as big or as small as you want.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: For the sake of this example, I'll just do like a week or two of days just to show you what's going on here.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And then the idea, it's called a dot plot, is you put some dots in each of the cells.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: You want to pick an event that your user does in the process of using your product that you think represents value in the product.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Maybe it's sharing a photo if you're building a photo app, or listening to a song if you're building a music app, or processing an invoice if you're building a B2B invoice processing product.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And you can just put a dot for each day that each user uses the product.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Let's say we're Spotify and we're building a music streaming app and we want to see how our users are using it.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Let's pick the event that we're going to chart here being listen to a song.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So anytime a user listens to a song during a day, we're going to put a dot.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So for me, let's say I...
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Listen to Spotify song on Monday and Tuesday and not on Wednesday, but Thursday and Friday again, and then maybe again on Monday and Wednesday.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Another thing you can do to make a record of the first day that a user used the product, the day that they onboarded, you can put another symbol.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Like let's say on a user's first day, we'll just draw a little ring around the dot like that just to give us a little bit more signal.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And what you'll eventually start seeing
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: is a pretty high density visualization of individual users and their usage over time.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: What's really cool about this is it lets you figure out patterns
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: That you probably would not have seen with your human brain just looking at aggregate charts or looking at individual user logs.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Okay, so let's look at this example I've just drawn.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: For our Spotify app, what do we see?
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: What patterns have emerged now that we can see individual users and their own behavior?
speaker: SPEAKER_01

speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: We've got myself, we've got user number three here, user four used it on a Monday, user six used it during the week, and there's a couple users who seem to kind of only use it on the weekends.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Do I want the weekday work time listeners or do I want the weekend users?
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: We would have no idea about this if we didn't have a dot plot visualization like this.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Another thing I can see is...
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: A measure of retention.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Like, do we see a lot of users like User4 that try the app on one day and then never come back?
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: If we see that on a bunch of our rows, we have an idea of a potential problem that we've got in our onboarding or other things.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: As you get more sophisticated with dot plots, you can make them as intricate as you want.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: At Bump, we had different symbols that we would put into these cells.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So we knew whether you shared your contact information using Bomb or if you shared a photo.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And it gives you a lot more granularity.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And you can kind of go as deep as you want on this.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

speaker: SPEAKER_01

speaker: SPEAKER_01

speaker: SPEAKER_01

speaker: SPEAKER_01

speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Is this a user that makes a lot of money?
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Or is this a college kid that you just got on Reddit or something?
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: You can encode those states with other symbols or shading the cells different colors.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: You can write things over here.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So like I might say, this is an iOS user, and this is an iOS user, but these ones are Androids.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And another thing you can do then is sort your rows based on whatever attributes you want to sort them by.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So you might say, I only want to look at iOS users first, or I only want to look at users whose first time using the app was this Monday.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So let's resort so we only see people that have rings around their first day.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: What you find when you look at this in aggregate, you can then kind of zoom out and see an entire page of these, is your brain will start to notice these patterns.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: In a way that you would never have figured out on your own a priori.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: This is actually an idea that I remember hearing about 10 years ago from Max Levchin, one of the founders of PayPal.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: They had a big fraud problem at PayPal when they first launched, but they didn't know the patterns to look for.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So what they did instead is build a visualization, a graph of all the transactions that were happening on PayPal.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And they just had humans sit and stare at screens of these drawings and graphs.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And while the humans didn't know what exactly was going on, they were able to look at the screen and say, that thing happening there, that's different and probably fraud.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And then they would go and dig into that.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: It's kind of the same idea with dot plots.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: You can look at these charts and figure out, huh.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: There's something going on with users.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: I see this pattern emerging.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And then you can go dig into it a lot deeper.

speaker: SPEAKER_01

speaker: SPEAKER_01

speaker: SPEAKER_01

speaker: SPEAKER_01

speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And you might start to see patterns.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Where specific features maybe drive behaviors in the product that you actually want.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Let's just say for the sake of argument that we see this one user here that joined a public playlist.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: They then have a string of many, many consecutive days of using the product.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: We could then infer like, oh, maybe the playlist feature is really causal to having people be really active in our product.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: This is the sort of stuff that you can learn with dot plots.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So what's really great for most founders, you have a very small number of users at the beginning.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And so you can literally look at every single user of your product on every single day they've ever used it.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And it all fits on one screen on your monitor.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: That's really great.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: But it actually does scale to when you have thousands or millions or billions of users.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: This is a tool that we used at Google Photos when we had well more than a billion users.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And the idea is you can just choose to sample your users and represent them on a dot plot however you want.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So we would have days where we print out dozens of these pieces of paper with dot plots on them for different samples of our user base.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: I would print out a piece of paper and hand one of our team members like, here's the iOS users in France.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: I want you to understand what they're doing.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Let's see what they're up to.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And we would have days where we just sit in the office and look at these dot plots and try to draw conclusions about what's going on with our users.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

speaker: SPEAKER_01

speaker: SPEAKER_01

speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And it turns out what happened is the company was in the States.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

speaker: SPEAKER_01

speaker: SPEAKER_01

speaker: SPEAKER_01

speaker: SPEAKER_01

speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So there's a few ways you can misuse dot plots.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: The number one thing is to just chart the wrong event.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: A lot of founders might want to populate their dot plot with the easiest way to populate it so it feels good and you see a lot of dots.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Maybe you'll pick, like, opened the app or signed into the product.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Those are pretty bad events to choose because they don't really measure whether the user is getting real value.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So I suggest you pick something that actually represents value being created for the user.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Listen to a song, share a photo, something like that that's a real event.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: The other mistake you can make is picking a time period that's too wide.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Sometimes founders want to make it look better and they pick weeks, like week one, week two, week three.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: It's way harder to figure out what's actually going on unless you look at it at the day or maybe even like sub-day granularity.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So I would go so far as to say until you have hundreds of users, the dot plot could be your only dashboard.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: What's great about dot plots is they're just a logs visualization tool.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: There's no fancy computations happening here.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: You basically just need to parse your logs and put them into a 2D grid.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: This is a thing that modern AI coding tools can whip up in like 10 minutes.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: These are best used in conjunction with cohort retention curves.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Cohort retention curves teach you in aggregate whether groups of users that you acquire stick with you over time.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: That's very important.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: You should definitely be measuring that.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: But the dot plot shows you how those users are actually using your product, and they give you the color to go ask the right questions of your users, to go build the right features, to fix things that are broken in your product that you would never learn by looking at aggregate metrics.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So cohort retention curves and dot plots are, in my experience, two of the most important tools that you've got to understand your users.
